facts.claim: As at November 2026, Smartraveller's Greece advice (read live 12 November 2026; 'Still current at 13 November 2026', updated 30 September 2026), Local laws summary: 'Same-sex relationships are legal, though attitudes vary throughout the country. Avoid public displays of affection, especially in rural areas. Attitudes are generally more accepting on Greek islands such as Mykonos, Santorini and Ios.'

As at November 2026, Smartraveller's Greece advice, Local customs section (read live 12 November 2026): 'Avoid public displays of affection, especially in rural areas. Same-sex relationships are legal but isn't widely accepted.' The section links to Smartraveller's 'Advice for LGBTQIA+ people'.

As at November 2026, Smartraveller's Greece advice, Safety section (read live 12 November 2026): 'Racially motivated and homophobic attacks have occurred.' It also says serious physical and sexual assaults have occurred in Athens and on islands including Mykonos, Santorini, Zakynthos and Ios, and there is a risk of drink spiking.

As at November 2026, Smartraveller's Greece advice (read live 12 November 2026): if your Australian passport has an 'X' in the sex field, the Australian Government can't guarantee entry or transit to other countries; ask the embassy or consulate of your destinations whether they will accept it, and check all transit destinations too.

As at November 2026, Smartraveller's Greece advice (read live 12 November 2026) has no section on getting married; marriage steps must come from the Australian Embassy in Athens, Smartraveller's 'Getting married overseas' page and Greek official sources.

As at November 2026, Smartraveller's Greece advice (read live 12 November 2026): Greece is in the Schengen area; Australians can travel to the Schengen area for short trips without a visa for up to 90 days in any 180-day period; on arrival for a short stay on an Australian passport you register fingerprints and a photo under the European Entry/Exit System (EES), which is free and needs no action before arrival, and there may be delays at border crossings.

As at November 2026, Smartraveller 'Getting married overseas' (last updated 18/08/2026, read live 12 November 2026): some countries ask you to prove you aren't already married; the most common documents are a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI) and certificates from a registry of births, deaths and marriages; the country may have more rules (for example a residence period); 'We can't tell you what you will need'; contact your destination's embassy or consulate. The Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements.

As at November 2026, Smartraveller 'Getting married overseas' (read live 12 November 2026): your registry of births, deaths and marriages can give a statement that there's no record you have been married before, a Single Status certificate or a No Record Result certificate; local authorities may also ask for divorce papers, the death certificate of a deceased spouse, and your original birth certificate and passport.

As at November 2026, Smartraveller 'Getting married overseas' (read live 12 November 2026): Australia doesn't recognise overseas marriages where one or both people are already married to someone else, not old enough to get married, too closely related, or forced to get married.

As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department 'Marriage equality in Australia' page (read live 12 November 2026; page metadata updated 3 December 2025): since 9 December 2017 the Marriage Act 1961 defines marriage as 'the union of 2 people to the exclusion of all others, voluntarily entered into for life', and 'same-sex marriages that took place overseas are generally recognised in Australia.' The Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements.

As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department (read live 12 November 2026): if Australia recognises your overseas marriage, you can't get married again in Australia, but you may choose to hold another type of ceremony, such as a confirmation of vows or a recommitment ceremony.

As at November 2026, the Attorney-General's Department (read live 12 November 2026): from 9 December 2017 same-sex married couples are treated the same as other married couples in Australia, whether the marriage happened before or after that date, or overseas (if Australia would recognise it as a valid overseas marriage). Contact: Marriage Law and Celebrants Section, 1800 550 343, outside Australia +61 2 6141 3111.

As at November 2026, the Australian Embassy in Athens notarial services page (read live 11 November 2026) lists witnessing application forms for, and issuing, Certificates of No Impediment (CNI), witnessing notices of intended marriage, and legalisation of signatures and/or seals by authentication or apostille. An appointment is needed for all notarial services (Monday to Friday, 9:00am to 12:30pm), though apostille and CNI documents can be submitted by post; legalised (apostilled) documents and CNIs are available for collection within two working days unless same-day collection is arranged in advance, or can be returned by mail. A fee applies. The Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements. [Copied from mykonos-wedding part-1 fact_104.] [Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding part-1 fact_103.]

As at November 2026, the Australian Embassy in Athens (read live 11 November 2026) says it does not provide legal advice, the client is responsible for knowing which service they need, it does not witness signatures on overseas documents (ask local authorities who can witness, or get legal advice), and honorary consuls are not authorised to provide notarial services. [Copied from mykonos-wedding part-1 fact_105.] [Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding part-1 fact_104.]

Australian Embassy, Athens: 5 Hatziyianni Mexi Street, Athens 115 28; phone +30 210 870 4000; greece.embassy.gov.au. [Copied from greek-wedding-traditions part-1 fact_102.] [Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding part-1 fact_105.]

As at November 2026, Smartraveller (read live 11 November 2026) says DFAT can issue a CNI in Australia, but some local authorities only accept CNIs issued in their country, so ask the destination's embassy or consulate whether you need a CNI, whether you can get it in Australia, and whether it also needs an authentication or apostille. The Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements. [Copied from mykonos-wedding part-1 fact_101.] [Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding part-1 fact_106.]

As at November 2026, Smartraveller (read live 11 November 2026) says you cannot register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is legally recognised if, when it took place, it was valid under the law of the country where it happened and would have been valid under Australian law had it occurred in Australia. A foreign marriage certificate is usually accepted as proof of the marriage but may not work as proof of a name change (check with your local registry of births, deaths and marriages), and Smartraveller suggests talking to a lawyer to confirm the certificate is valid in Australia. The Wedded Advisor confirms current requirements. [Copied from mykonos-wedding part-1 fact_102.] [Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding part-1 fact_108.]
Smartraveller advises dressing modestly in churches and religious buildings in Greece. [Copied from greek-wedding-traditions part-1 fact_103.] [Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding part-1 fact_110.]

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: weddings are performed by a Priest recognised as canonical by the Archdiocese; the laws and regulations for weddings are set by the Holy Canons of the Orthodox Church and implemented by the Archdiocese, and apply to every Greek Orthodox Priest across Australia. [Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding part-3 fact_310.]

Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia: the crowning is the climax of the Marriage Service; the crowns are a sign of the bond between bride and groom and represent the glory and honour God bestows on the couple. Crowns were usually plaited of lemon blossoms or flowers; today they are often silver or gold. The Best Man exchanges the crowns three times while the Priest and Chanter sing 'Lord our God, crown them in glory and honour.' [Copied from greek-orthodox-wedding part-3 fact_304.]

The Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia's marriage page (Laws & Regulations) states: 'The sacramental union of a man and a woman is performed in an Orthodox Church according to the liturgical tradition, and blessed by a Priest who is recognised as canonical (authentic) by the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia.' Its Ceremony of Marriage section says marriage is a Sacrament 'through which the union of man and woman is sanctified by God.'

insider_details.detail: Order the paperwork from both ends early: Smartraveller says DFAT can issue a CNI in Australia but some authorities only accept ones issued locally, and the Embassy in Athens needs an appointment (weekday mornings) for notarial work, though CNI paperwork can go by post. Ask the municipality which version it accepts before booking flights.

Once married in Greece, you can't marry each other again in Australia if the marriage is recognised, so a home celebration should be framed as a recommitment or confirmation of vows, not a second wedding.

Plan guest comfort around the island: Smartraveller says attitudes are generally more accepting on Mykonos, Santorini and Ios and advises avoiding public displays of affection in rural areas, so keep mainland or village excursions in mind when planning the welcome and farewell events.

Brief the wedding party on safety without alarm: Smartraveller notes homophobic attacks and drink spiking have occurred, including on the main islands, so organise transfers back to the hotel after the reception rather than leaving guests to find late-night taxis.

Check passports for every guest: Smartraveller warns that an 'X' sex marker can't be guaranteed for entry or transit, and the EES border registration can cause queues, so guests should check transit countries and allow extra time on arrival.
